Gymnosperms. These are seed-bearing plants, and their seeds develop naked, exposed directly to the air rather than being enclosed in any kind of fruit. The group includes conifers like pines, firs, and spruce, as well as cycads, ginkgos, and gnetophytes. For over two hundred million years, gymnosperms dominated terrestrial ecosystems before flowering plants eventually rose to prominence.

The defining feature is that the seeds sit exposed on the surface of a cone scale or equivalent structure, which is what distinguishes them from angiosperm seeds that are enclosed inside an ovary. All gymnosperms possess vascular tissue and are woody, with a durable secondary growth pattern that creates those tree rings you see in conifers.

When it comes to reproduction, gymnosperms use pollination, where wind-blown pollen delivers sperm to the egg, and this eliminated any dependence on free water. The gametophyte is microscopic and housed entirely within the seed. There are four major groups: the Coniferophyta, which includes pines, firs, and spruces and is by far the most diverse; the Cycadophyta, which are palm-like and quite ancient; the Ginkgophyta, represented today by just one surviving species, the ginkgo itself; and the Gnetophyta, which are rare and have varied forms.

Gymnosperms dominated the Mesozoic Era, the age of dinosaurs, and conifers remain ecologically dominant today in cool or harsh climates, particularly in boreal forests and on high mountains. Many conifers produce resin and other secondary metabolites that deter herbivores and serve as commercial products like turpentine and pitch. Gymnosperms evolved from fern-like ancestors by acquiring seeds, so spores became enclosed inside seeds rather than being broadcast to the air, and from these early gymnosperms, flowering plants eventually evolved by adding flowers and fruits.
